## Conclusion

The state should raise the posted limit on its eleven rural interstate segments from 65 to 75 mph. Traffic on those segments already moves at 74 mph at the 85th percentile, so the posted number no longer describes how the road is used [1]. Federal guidance treats the 85th-percentile operating speed as the primary input to a posted limit and a limit set far below that speed as one that will be neither obeyed nor enforced evenly [2]. The strongest objection to the change is that a higher number simply resets the reference point and the 85th percentile climbs again; the measured record bounds that effect rather than dismissing it, which is why the recommendation stands [3].

## Key findings

- The 85th-percentile operating speed across the eleven affected segments is 74 mph against a 65 mph posted limit, and the median is 71 mph [1].
- Federal guidance names the 85th percentile as the primary input to a posted limit, with documented engineering adjustments applied on top of it [2].
- Where posted limits have been raised elsewhere, measured operating speeds moved by roughly a quarter to a half of the posted change rather than one for one [3].
- Citations issued per patrol-mile vary by more than a factor of ten between highway patrol districts, and 68 percent of them are written on four of the eleven segments [4].

## The strongest counterargument

The serious objection is that a posted limit functions as a reference point rather than as a rule, so moving the number moves the whole distribution with it: drivers who treated 65 as advisory would treat 75 the same way, the 85th percentile would settle near 82, and the state would be back where it started with a faster baseline. On that reading the change buys nothing and has to be repeated every few years.

The surveyed record bounds the effect rather than eliminating it. Across the posted-limit increases reviewed in the federal practice literature, operating speeds rose by a fraction of the posted change rather than tracking it, and the resulting 85th percentile settled below the new posted value [3]. The objection therefore survives as a reason to re-measure operating speeds two years after any change and to publish the result — a commitment the department should make in the rulemaking itself — but not as a prediction that the distribution simply follows the sign.

## What the posted limit describes today

The department's 2024 speed study instrumented all eleven segments with pneumatic tube counters for fourteen consecutive days each, recording free-flow passenger-vehicle speeds only; readings taken in queued or weather-affected conditions were discarded before the percentiles were computed [1]. Pneumatic road tubes are the standard portable method for short-duration vehicle speed data collection in FHWA traffic-monitoring practice, and the department's protocol follows it [5]. The 85th percentile came out at 74 mph and the median at 71 mph, nine and six miles per hour above the posted limit respectively.

The gap is stable rather than episodic. It varies by less than 2 mph between daytime and overnight windows and by less than 3 mph across the four measurement months, and no single segment accounts for it: the narrowest per-segment gap in the study is 7 mph [1]. A posted limit that essentially all free-flow traffic exceeds is describing something other than how the road is driven.

## How a posted limit is set

Federal practice guidance describes the 85th-percentile operating speed as the starting point for a posted limit, adjusted from there for documented engineering factors — interchange and access density, horizontal curvature, and available sight distance — with each adjustment recorded in the speed-study file [2]. The eleven segments are rural, grade-separated and of uniform cross-section, and the department's file records no adjustment on any of them.

The current 65 mph posting predates the 2019 reconstruction of the corridor and was carried forward unchanged when the reconstruction was accepted [1]. Nothing in the file indicates that the number was re-derived after the geometry changed; it is an inherited value rather than a measured one.

## Enforcement

Enforcement of the current limit is concentrated and uneven. Citations per patrol-mile differ by more than a factor of ten between the patrol districts covering the corridor, and 68 percent of all citations written on the eleven segments in fiscal 2024 came from four of them [4].

That pattern follows from the gap. When most free-flow traffic exceeds the posted limit, a patrol officer is selecting from a very large pool of technically violating drivers rather than identifying an unusual one, and which drivers are selected becomes a function of where patrols are assigned [4]. A posted limit closer to the operating speed narrows that pool and makes the selection less arbitrary.

## Travel time

The travel-time case is weak and the recommendation does not rest on it. If operating speeds rise by the fraction the surveyed increases suggest — roughly 3 mph on top of the current 74 — the saving over the full 120-mile corridor is about three minutes [3]. Any argument for this change that leads with driver time is overstating what the measured record supports.
